subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which best describes the logical structure of a direct deductive proof?
options: work from known facts step by step to the conclusion
assume the negation and find a contradiction
questions.explain: Deduction chains established facts and definitions to reach the conclusion.

questions.q: Which is a valid counter-example to 'n^2 > n for all integers n'?
questions.explain: At n=1, n^2=1 which is not greater than 1, so it fails.

questions.q: Which is a counter-example to 'n^2 - n + 41 is prime for all positive integers n'?
questions.explain: At n=41, n^2-n+41=41(41) which is divisible by 41, hence not prime.

questions.q: To disprove the statement 'all primes are odd', the best approach is:
questions.explain: A single counter-example such as 2 disproves a universal statement.

questions.q: A flawed proof concludes 1=2 after assuming a=b and dividing by (a-b). The error is:
questions.explain: Since a=b, the factor a-b is zero and cannot be divided by.

questions.q: Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes is a proof by:
questions.explain: It assumes finitely many primes and reaches a contradiction.

questions.q: A counter-example to 'if n is prime then n is odd' is:
questions.explain: 2 is prime but even, disproving the statement.

questions.q: Which statement is the contrapositive of 'if P then Q'?
options: P if and only if Q
if not P then not Q
if not Q then not P
questions.explain: The contrapositive is 'if not Q then not P' and is logically equivalent.

questions.q: 'P is equivalent to Q' is best written using which connective?
questions.explain: Equivalence means 'if and only if' (both implications hold).

questions.q: A counter-example to 'every quadratic equation has two real roots' is:
questions.explain: x^2+1=0 has no real roots, disproving the claim.

questions.q: Which method proves a statement by checking every possible case?
questions.explain: Proof by exhaustion checks all cases individually.

questions.q: In 'P implies Q', Q is described as a ____ condition for P.
questions.explain: Q must hold whenever P does, so Q is necessary for P.

questions.q: In a proof by exhaustion of a statement about remainders mod 3, how many cases must be checked?
questions.explain: Every integer leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 mod 3, giving 3 cases.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid method of mathematical proof?
questions.explain: A single supporting example does not prove a general statement.

questions.q: To prove a statement true for all integers n from 1 to 5 by testing each value is:
questions.explain: Checking each case in a finite set is proof by exhaustion.

questions.q: To prove 'the sum of two consecutive integers is odd', writing them as n and n+1 then summing to 2n+1 is:
questions.explain: It derives the result directly using algebra, i.e. deduction.

questions.q: 'x>3' is a ____ condition for 'x>2'.
questions.explain: x>3 guarantees x>2 but x>2 does not require x>3, so it is sufficient only.

questions.q: In 'P implies Q', P is described as a ____ condition for Q.
questions.explain: If P implies Q, then P being true is sufficient for Q.

questions.q: To prove 'if x^2 is even then x is even', the cleanest approach is:
options: contrapositive (if x is odd then x^2 is odd)
questions.explain: Proving the equivalent contrapositive is the standard clean method here.

questions.q: Which statement is the converse of 'if P then Q'?
options: if not P then not Q
if not Q then not P
questions.explain: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion: if Q then P.

questions.q: The proof that sqrt(2) is irrational is a classic example of:
questions.explain: It assumes sqrt(2) is rational and derives a contradiction.

questions.q: Proof by contradiction begins by assuming:
options: the opposite of what you want to prove
questions.explain: You assume the negation, then derive a contradiction.

questions.q: In the sqrt(2) proof, we assume sqrt(2)=a/b where a/b is:
questions.explain: Assuming lowest terms lets the shared factor of 2 give a contradiction.

questions.q: 'P if and only if Q' means:
options: both P implies Q and Q implies P
questions.explain: An iff statement asserts both directions of implication.

questions.q: A counter-example to 'the product of two irrational numbers is always irrational' is:
questions.explain: sqrt(2) x sqrt(2) = 2, which is rational, disproving the claim.

questions.q: 'A shape is a square' is ____ for 'it is a rectangle'.
questions.explain: Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square, so square is sufficient.

questions.q: A single valid counter-example to a 'for all' statement shows the statement is:
questions.explain: One counter-example is enough to make a universal statement false.

questions.q: A flawed 'proof' that divides both sides of an equation by (a-b) is invalid when:
questions.explain: Dividing by a-b is division by zero when a=b, which is not allowed.

questions.q: To prove 'if n is even then n^2 is even', writing n=2k and showing n^2=4k^2 is an example of:
questions.explain: It works directly from definitions to the conclusion, i.e. deduction.

questions.q: 'A number is divisible by 6' is ____ for 'it is divisible by 3'.
questions.explain: Divisibility by 6 guarantees divisibility by 3, but 3 itself shows it is not necessary.
